claim: Brachypodium distachyon accessions cluster into three main genetic lineages (the A, B, and C genetic lineages), which further divide into five main genetic clades that display little evidence for historical gene flow.
source: Recent genetic studies based on more than 320 natural accessions spanning from Spain to Iraq (hereafter referred to as the B. distachyon diversity panel) revealed that B. distachyon accessions cluster into three main genetic lineages (the A, B, and C genetic lineages), which further divide into five main genetic clades that display little evidence for historical gene flow (Figure 1A; Stritt et al., 2022; Minadakis et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Stritt et al., 2022 and Minadakis et al., 2023, and referenced in Figure 1A

claim: B. distachyon moved southward during the last glacial period and recolonized Europe and the Middle East within the last five thousand years.
source: Niche modeling analyses suggest that the species moved southward during the last glacial period and recolonized Europe and the Middle East within the last five thousand years (Minadakis et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Minadakis et al., 2023 and niche modeling analyses

claim: 97,660 TE polymorphisms were identified in the B. distachyon dataset, of which 9,172 were retrotransposons, 52,249 were DNA-transposons and 36,239 were unclassified.
source: Using the B. distachyon diversity panel (Figure 1A), we identified 97,660 TE polymorphisms in our B. distachyon dataset, of which 9172 were retrotransposons, 52,249 were DNA-transposons and 36,239 were unclassified.
evidence: Direct observation from the dataset analyzed in this study

claim: 9 million SNPs were identified across the 326 samples, including 182,801 synonymous SNPs.
source: We also identified 9 million SNPs across the 326 samples, including 182,801 synonymous SNPs.
evidence: Direct observation from the dataset analyzed in this study

claim: The observed diversity in retrotransposons strongly correlated with the demographic structure (Mantel test; r=0.79, p-value = 0.001).
source: Investigating the genetic variation caused by retrotransposons and DNA-transposons revealed that the observed diversity in retrotransposons strongly correlated with the demographic structure (Mantel test; r=0.79, p-value = 0.001)
evidence: Statistical test (Mantel test) performed on the data

claim: The observed diversity in DNA-transposons only had a weaker correlation (Mantel test; r=0.36, p-value = 0.001) with the demographic structure.
source: while the observed diversity in DNA-transposons only had a weaker correlation (Mantel test; r=0.36, p-value = 0.001) with the demographic structure (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Statistical test (Mantel test) performed on the data and shown in supplementary figure

claim: The age of 50,891 TE polymorphisms and 108,855 synonymous SNPs was estimated based on pairwise differences in identity by descent (IBD) regions around the focal mutation.
source: From the initial TE and SNP dataset, we could estimate the time of origin in generations (age) of 50,891 TE polymorphisms and 108,855 synonymous SNPs based on pairwise differences in identity by descent (IBD) regions around the focal mutation (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Methodological approach described and applied to the dataset

claim: The observed correlation between allele age and frequency of synonymous SNPs matched theoretical predictions for neutrally evolving mutations.
source: We found that, the observed correlation matched expectations (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), with older alleles found on average at higher frequencies than younger ones.
evidence: Comparison of observed data to theoretical predictions from Kimura and Ohta, 1973

claim: Most TE polymorphisms in the dataset were young and only a few were very old.
source: Furthermore, most TE polymorphisms in our dataset were young and only a few were very old (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Direct observation from age distribution analysis shown in supplementary figure

claim: The number of fixed TE polymorphisms per clade did not significantly differ between high iHS regions and the same regions in other clades.
source: An analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) revealed that the number of fixed TE polymorphisms per clade did not significantly differ between high iHS regions and the same regions in other clades (Table 1).
evidence: ANCOVA statistical analysis performed on the data

claim: The number of fixed TEs in genomic regions was significantly affected by the total number of TEs in the region, the TE superfamily, the TE age, the genetic clade and the overall genetic features of the region but not by the iHS itself.
source: However, the number of fixed TEs in genomic regions along the genome was significantly affected by the total number of TEs in the region, the TE superfamily, the TE age, the genetic clade and the overall genetic features of the region (e.g. recombination rate, see Materials and methods) but not by the iHS itself (Table 1).
evidence: ANCOVA statistical analysis results shown in Table 1

claim: The allele frequency of TE polymorphisms was significantly influenced by the TE superfamily, TE age, clade and overall genetic features of the region but not by the iHS.
source: A second ANCOVA revealed that the allele frequency of TE polymorphisms was significantly influenced by the TE superfamily, TE age, clade and overall genetic features of the region but not by the iHS (Table 2).
evidence: ANCOVA statistical analysis results shown in Table 2

claim: Only a small fraction of the TE polymorphisms (0.06%) displayed XtX values higher than the 97.5% quantile of the simulated values.
source: We contrasted the observed XtX values computed for each TE polymorphism to a simulated pseudo-observed dataset (simulated observations under the demographic model inferred from the covariance matrix of the SNP dataset, for more details see Olazcuaga et al., 2020) and found that only a small fraction of the TE polymorphisms (0.06%) displayed XtX values higher than the 97.5% quantile of the simulated values (Figure 1B).
evidence: XtX analysis comparing observed to simulated data

claim: A relatively larger portion of the TE polymorphisms (4.3%) displayed XtX values smaller than the 2.5% quantile of the simulated values.
source: However, a relatively larger portion of the TE polymorphisms (4.3%) displayed XtX values smaller than the 2.5% quantile of the simulated values (Figure 1B), indicating that balancing selection might also shape TE frequency in B. distachyon.
evidence: XtX analysis comparing observed to simulated data

claim: Only nine of the 97,660 TE polymorphisms were significantly associated with environmental factors.
source: The GEA revealed that only nine of the 97,660 TE polymorphisms were significantly associated with some environmental factors (Supplementary file 1-table 1c), confirming that TEs only had a limited contribution to adaptation in B. distachyon.
evidence: Genome-environment association analysis results

claim: Two of the nine TEs significantly associated with environmental factors were found in a gene, and three were in the vicinity of genes (less than 2 kb away).
source: Importantly, two of these nine TEs were found in a gene, and three were in the vicinity of genes (less than 2 kilobase (kb) away, Supplementary file 1-table 1c).
evidence: Direct observation from the GEA results

claim: The folded SFS of TE polymorphisms was shifted toward a higher proportion of rare minor alleles compared to neutral sites in all genetic clades.
source: We first computed the folded site frequency spectrum (SFS) and found that the folded SFS of TE polymorphisms was shifted toward a higher proportion of rare minor alleles compared to neutral sites in all genetic clades (Figure 1C–G).
evidence: Site frequency spectrum analysis shown in Figure 1C-G

claim: Older retrotransposons are significantly less frequent than neutral SNPs of the same age.
source: This analysis revealed that retrotransposons are indeed prevented by natural selection from randomly accumulating, as older retrotransposons are significantly less frequent than neutral SNPs of the same age (Figure 2; one-sided Wilcoxon test, Bonferroni corrected p-value <0.01).
evidence: Age-adjusted SFS analysis with statistical testing shown in Figure 2

claim: Older retrotransposon polymorphisms were significantly less frequent than neutral sites of the same age regardless of their distance to genes.
source: The age-adjusted SFS of all three categories displayed the same pattern as that observed for the whole retrotransposon polymorphism dataset: older retrotransposon polymorphisms were significantly less frequent than neutral sites of the same age regardless of their distance to genes (one-sided Wilcoxon test, Bonferroni corrected p-value <0.01), indicating that retrotransposons more than 5 kb away from genes are also affected by purifying selection (Figure 2).
evidence: Age-adjusted SFS analysis stratified by distance to genes with statistical testing

claim: Retrotransposon polymorphisms tended to be more deleterious than SNPs predicted to have a high impact on fitness.
source: Retrotransposon polymorphisms tended to be more deleterious than SNPs predicted to have a high impact on fitness. Indeed, the age-adjusted SFS of retrotransposons resulted in a larger deviation of Δ frequency from 0 than for non-synonymous SNPs and high effect SNPs (Figure 2).
evidence: Comparison of age-adjusted SFS between retrotransposons and different SNP categories

claim: In the A_East, B_East and B_west clades, Δ frequency in the oldest age bin was significantly more negative than in all other age bins.
source: In addition, Δ frequency in the oldest (last) age bin was significantly more negative than in all other age bins in the A_East, B_East and B_west clades (one-sided Wilcoxon test, Bonferroni corrected p-value <0.01).
evidence: Statistical testing of age-adjusted SFS data

claim: DNA-transposon polymorphisms seemed less deleterious than non-synonymous SNPs and high effect SNPs.
source: The age-adjusted SFS of DNA-transposons revealed very similar patterns, with Δ frequency showing significant deviations from 0 in older age bins (one-sided Wilcoxon test, Bonferroni corrected p-value <0.01), but DNA-transposon polymorphisms seemed less deleterious than non-synonymous SNPs and high effect SNPs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Age-adjusted SFS analysis for DNA-transposons shown in supplementary figure

claim: The shape of the age-adjusted SFS of retrotransposons could only be reproduced if less than 10% of the mutations were neutrally evolving for most of the selective constraint investigated.
source: Our simulations revealed that the shape of the age-adjusted SFS of retrotransposons could only be reproduced if less than 10% of the mutations were neutrally evolving for most of the selective constraint investigated (Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 1-table 1d).
evidence: Forward simulation results comparing different proportions of neutral mutations

claim: Simulations assuming a moderately weak selection pressure (S = –5 or S = –8) against TE polymorphisms best fitted the observed data.
source: Examining the age of the last retrotransposon bins in the age-adjusted SFS revealed that the ages of the oldest retrotransposons were the most similar to the expected ages of the oldest mutations in our simulations, with a scaled selection coefficient (S) of –5 and –8 (Figure 3), indicating that retrotransposons in B. distachyon are under moderate purifying selection.
evidence: Comparison of observed retrotransposon ages to simulated ages under different selection coefficients

claim: TEs account for approximately 30% of the B. distachyon genome.
source: In B. distachyon, TEs are exhaustively annotated and account for approximately 30% of the genome (International Brachypodium Initiative, 2010).
evidence: Cited from International Brachypodium Initiative, 2010

claim: Recent TE activity has been reported for many families in B. distachyon.
source: Recent TE activity has been reported for many families, but despite past independent bottlenecks and expansions experienced by the different genetic clades, no lineage-specific TE family activity has been observed (Lockton et al., 2008).
evidence: Cited from Lockton et al., 2008

claim: No lineage-specific TE family activity has been observed in B. distachyon despite past independent bottlenecks and expansions experienced by the different genetic clades.
source: Recent TE activity has been reported for many families, but despite past independent bottlenecks and expansions experienced by the different genetic clades, no lineage-specific TE family activity has been observed (Lockton et al., 2008).
evidence: Cited from Lockton et al., 2008

claim: TE activity tends to be homogeneous throughout the species range and across genetic clades in B. distachyon.
source: Rather, TE activity tends to be homogeneous throughout the species range and across genetic clades, indicating a high level of conservation of the TE regulatory apparatus (Lockton et al., 2008).
evidence: Cited from Lockton et al., 2008

claim: Purifying selection shapes the accumulation patterns of TEs in B. distachyon.
source: While purifying selection shapes the accumulation patterns of TEs in this species (Lockton et al., 2008), some TE polymorphisms have been observed in the vicinity of genes (Lockton et al., 2008), potentially affecting gene expression (Wyler et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from Lockton et al., 2008 and Wyler et al., 2020

claim: B. distachyon is a wild annual grass endemic to the Mediterranean basin and Middle East.
source: B. distachyon is a wild annual grass endemic to the Mediterranean basin and Middle East.
evidence: Established knowledge about the species

claim: The B. distachyon genome is 272 Mb in size.
source: it is not surprising that most new insertions interfere with the function of the genome, especially in a species with a small genome, such as B. distachyon (272 Mb) (International Brachypodium Initiative, 2010).
evidence: Cited from International Brachypodium Initiative, 2010

claim: 42.5% of the B. distachyon genome are genes.
source: Hence, the fact that only a small proportion of TEs can accumulate neutrally indicates that, in a gene-dense genome such as that of B. distachyon (42.5% of the genome are genes; Wyler et al., 2022), TE insertions in any genomic compartment may result in some cis- or trans-regulatory effects visible to selection.
evidence: Cited from Wyler et al., 2022

claim: B. distachyon displays a high selfing rate.
source: Because B. distachyon displays a high selfing rate (Stritt et al., 2022), most genetic variants are expected to be homozygous within an individual.
evidence: Cited from Stritt et al., 2022

claim: The selfing rate in B. distachyon was set to 70% in the simulations.
source: The selfing rate was set to 70%, as B. distachyon is a highly selfing species with occasional outcrossing (Stritt et al., 2022; Minadakis et al., 2023).
evidence: Parameter used in simulations based on citations

claim: TEs can alter phenotypes through functional disruption of genes.
source: TEs can alter phenotypes through various mechanisms, including the functional disruption of genes (Bhattacharyya et al., 1990; Hof et al., 2016)
evidence: Cited from Bhattacharyya et al., 1990 and Hof et al., 2016

claim: TEs can alter phenotypes through large-scale changes in the regulatory apparatus.
source: TEs can alter phenotypes through various mechanisms, including the functional disruption of genes (Bhattacharyya et al., 1990; Hof et al., 2016), large-scale changes in the regulatory apparatus (Feschotte, 2008; Qiu and Köhler, 2020)
evidence: Cited from Feschotte, 2008 and Qiu and Köhler, 2020

claim: TEs can alter phenotypes through alteration of epigenetic landscapes.
source: TEs can alter phenotypes through various mechanisms, including the functional disruption of genes (Bhattacharyya et al., 1990; Hof et al., 2016), large-scale changes in the regulatory apparatus (Feschotte, 2008; Qiu and Köhler, 2020), alteration of epigenetic landscapes (Slotkin and Martienssen, 2007; Hollister and Gaut, 2009)
evidence: Cited from Slotkin and Martienssen, 2007 and Hollister and Gaut, 2009

claim: TEs can alter phenotypes through ectopic recombination and structural rearrangements.
source: TEs can alter phenotypes through various mechanisms, including the functional disruption of genes (Bhattacharyya et al., 1990; Hof et al., 2016), large-scale changes in the regulatory apparatus (Feschotte, 2008; Qiu and Köhler, 2020), alteration of epigenetic landscapes (Slotkin and Martienssen, 2007; Hollister and Gaut, 2009), ectopic recombination and structural rearrangements (Xiao et al., 2008; Gordon et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from Xiao et al., 2008 and Gordon et al., 2017

claim: The dynamics of TE loss and proliferation play a major role in genome evolution in plants.
source: In plants, the dynamics of TE loss and proliferation play a major role in genome evolution (e.g. 9–12).
evidence: General statement supported by multiple citations

claim: TE transpositional activity can be stress-inducible.
source: Beyond their influence on genome structure, and given that their transpositional activity can be stress-inducible (for review Negi et al., 2016)
evidence: Cited from review by Negi et al., 2016

claim: TE polymorphisms can induce more extreme changes in gene expression than single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in plants.
source: TE polymorphisms can even induce more extreme changes in gene expression than single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in plants (Uzunović et al., 2019; Castanera et al., 2023).
evidence: Cited from Uzunović et al., 2019 and Castanera et al., 2023

claim: The persistence of TE polymorphisms within a genome without an uncontrolled accumulation can only be achieved if weak purifying selection is the main force governing TE evolution.
source: Based on simulations, it has been suggested that the persistence of TE polymorphisms within a genome without an uncontrolled accumulation, can only be achieved if weak purifying selection is the main force governing TE evolution (Charlesworth, 1991; Charlesworth et al., 1997; Charlesworth and Charlesworth, 1983; Charlesworth, 1996).
evidence: Cited from multiple Charlesworth publications based on simulations

claim: The number of fixed TE polymorphisms per clade and the frequency of TE polymorphisms were negatively correlated with Ne.
source: In B. distachyon, the number of fixed TE polymorphisms per clade and the frequency of TE polymorphisms were negatively correlated with Ne, indicating that the accumulation of TEs is significantly lower in genetic clades with a larger Ne, potentially because of a greater efficacy of purifying selection.
evidence: Observed correlation from ANCOVA analysis

claim: The first two axes of the PCA based on TE polymorphisms explain less than 7% of the variance.
source: However, and in line with our simulations, the first two axes of the PCA explain less than 7% of the variance, indicating that neutrally evolving TEs contribute only mildly to overall TE diversity in our system.
evidence: PCA analysis results

claim: In A. thaliana, TEs located in the vicinity of genes (less than 2 kb) globally result in downregulation.
source: In A. thaliana, for instance, TEs located in the vicinity of genes (less than 2 kb) globally result in downregulation (Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from Wang et al., 2013

claim: Only specific TE families alter gene expression in B. distachyon.
source: Although only specific families alter gene expression in B. distachyon (Wyler et al., 2020), the observed Δ frequency for retrotransposon polymorphisms in genes and in their 1 kb surroundings matched our expectations.
evidence: Cited from Wyler et al., 2020

claim: TEs are believed to affect gene expression in trans through the production of small-interfering RNA in plants.
source: In plants, TEs are believed to affect gene expression in trans through the production of small-interfering RNA (McCue et al., 2013; McCue et al., 2012; McCue and Slotkin, 2012; Cho, 2018; Wyler et al., 2022).
evidence: Cited from multiple publications on TE-mediated gene regulation

claim: Putatively adaptive TE polymorphisms are rare in wild B. distachyon populations.
source: Using sequencing data from more than 320 natural B. distachyon accessions and a suite of population genomics approaches, we reveal that putatively adaptive TE polymorphisms are rare in wild B. distachyon populations.
evidence: Summary of multiple analyses including iHS, XtX, and GEA

claim: Only a small proportion of TE polymorphisms evolved neutrally (<10%) in B. distachyon.
source: After accounting for changes in past TE activity, we show that only a small proportion of TE polymorphisms evolved neutrally (<10%), while the vast majority of them are under moderate purifying selection regardless of their distance to genes.
evidence: Results from forward simulations and age-adjusted SFS analyses

claim: The vast majority of TE polymorphisms are under moderate purifying selection regardless of their distance to genes in B. distachyon.
source: After accounting for changes in past TE activity, we show that only a small proportion of TE polymorphisms evolved neutrally (<10%), while the vast majority of them are under moderate purifying selection regardless of their distance to genes.
evidence: Results from age-adjusted SFS analyses and simulations

claim: TEs are not favored during evolution and adaptation over other types of mutations (such as point mutations) in B. distachyon.
source: However, our study clearly shows that while they have a large potential to cause phenotypic variation in B. distachyon, they are not favored during evolution and adaptation over other types of mutations (such as point mutations) in this species.
evidence: Synthesis of multiple analyses showing limited adaptive role of TEs

claim: The B. distachyon diversity panel consists of 326 accessions.
source: In this study, we analyzed a total of 326 publicly available whole-genome sequencing data from Brachypodium distachyon accessions sampled around the Mediterranean Basin (Figure 1A; Supplementary file 1-table 1e).
evidence: Description of the dataset used in the study

claim: The B. distachyon dataset consisted of samples from five different published studies.
source: Our B. distachyon dataset consisted of 47 samples published by Gordon et al., 2017, 57 samples published by Skalska et al., 2020, 65 samples published by Gordon et al., 2020, 86 samples published by Stritt et al., 2022 and 71 samples published by Minadakis et al., 2023, covering all five genetic clades previously described in this species (Stritt et al., 2022; Minadakis et al., 2023).
evidence: Description of data sources with citations

claim: TIPs that were less than 100 base pairs apart in different samples and assigned to the same TE family were merged.
source: TIPs that were less than 100 base pairs (bp) apart in different samples and assigned to the same TE family were merged.
evidence: Methodological detail of data processing

claim: All TE calls were treated as homozygous in the analysis.
source: Because B. distachyon displays a high selfing rate (Stritt et al., 2022), most genetic variants are expected to be homozygous within an individual. Hence, all TE calls were treated as homozygous, and heterozygous SNP calls were removed from our dataset to reduce false variant calls.
evidence: Methodological decision based on biological characteristics of the species

claim: The C clade was identified as the most ancestral B. distachyon clade.
source: To estimate the age of each SNP and TE polymorphism, the SNPs and TEs found in the A_East, A_Italia, B_East and B_West clades were polarized using the C clade, which was identified as the most ancestral B. distachyon clade (Stritt et al., 2022) and used as the outgroup throughout this study.
evidence: Cited from Stritt et al., 2022

claim: A mutation rate of 7x10^-9 substitutions/generation was used for age estimation in B. distachyon.
source: GEVA was run separately for each clade using the genetic map produced by Huo et al., 2011 and a mutation rate of 7x10–9 substitutions/generation.
evidence: Methodological parameter used in GEVA analysis
